name: Dunhuang / Mogao visual tradition
region: Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, Gansu, China
summary: A multi-century cave-temple tradition shaped by Buddhism and Silk Road exchange. “Dunhuang style” is too broad for strict reconstruction.

social_roles.text: modern sitter translated into mural language

wardrobe.text: garment/iconography must follow chosen cave/subperiod and role; do not mix deity, donor and court costume casually

textiles_materials.text: painted cave-wall surface with layered preparation and mineral/earth pigments as a visual-material abstraction

hairstyle_headwear.text: iconographic hair/headwear varies widely by subject and period

architecture.text: rock-cut cave-temple interior and painted architectural illusion

musical_instruments.text: celestial/musical imagery is strongly represented but instrument choice should follow the chosen mural source family

writing_calligraphy.text: inscriptions and sutra context exist; never invent pseudo-script when readable text is expected

ritual_custom.text: Buddhist devotional/iconographic context is central; avoid casually turning a living subject into a sacred figure without explicit intent

lighting_technology.text: generated “golden divine light” is an interpretive visual device, not evidence of original cave illumination

visual_arts.text: large mural cycles and painted sculpture
Silk Road cultural exchange visible across centuries

incompatible_or_anachronistic.text: fully intact saturated surface labeled excavated/aged without conservation rationale

prompt_fragments.mural: Translate the subject into a wall-bound painted figure: flattened but graceful contour logic, mineral/earth pigment behavior, plaster/cave-wall texture, period-specific iconographic restraint, and physically plausible age state.

sources.supports: Mogao scope, murals, chronology and cultural exchange
workshop transfer/pouncing evidence for a Dunhuang mural fragment

scope_note: Foundation pack: use as a bounded starting point, not an encyclopedia.
strict_reconstruction_note: Strict mode requires a specific cave/subperiod or a tightly defined evidence family. Do not treat “Dunhuang” as a single era.
